newsitem.title: USA: Orange County, Calif., launches Wall Street tour.
newsitem.headline: Orange County, Calif., launches Wall Street tour.

text.p: Top Orange County, Calif., officials will meet this week with Wall Street bankers and credit analysts, hoping to boost investor confidence in the county one year after it emerged from bankruptcy.

Orange County shocked Wall Street in December 1994 when it descended into bankruptcy after suffering losses of more than $1.6 billion on risky interest rate bets made by its once-respected treasurer, Robert Citron.
Since emerging from bankruptcy last June, county officials have sought to regain the support of investors scared off by the 18-month-long financial crisis.
This week, the county stepped up its public relations effort by dispatching a team of senior county officials to New York as part of a so-called investor "road show."
In addition to New York, county officials were scheduled to hold investor events in Boston, Chicago and San Francisco.

"We have a budget that makes sense, that balances the demands of our 2.6 million citizens. We have done significant restructuring in the last year," Board of Supervisors Chairman William Steiner said in an interview.
County officials said the "road show" would be used to highlight the county's proposed 1997-1998 budget and to tout the county's new debt management plan.

The county's chief executive officer, Jan Mittermeier, said her $3.67 billion spending plan for fiscal year 1997-1998 would fund a reserve for contingencies of about $15 million, up from just $3 million. She said the county hoped this year to boost the reserve to $20 million.
Under its new "Credit and Debt Management" plan, the county said it would set aside at least $15 million a year from its fund balances to help reduce county debt levels.
Last year, the county set aside $26 million from its 1996-1997 fund balance. By the end of this June, the county said it should have $50 million set aside.
The "Credit and Debt Management" plan calls for the county to build up a $140 million fund by fiscal year 2001-2002 to retire or defease outstanding county bonds, officials said.
Christopher Varelas, a Salomon Brothers vice president and the county's senior financial advisor, said these efforts would improve the county's image on Wall Street and could lead to rating upgrades.
"The perception is going to improve," he said. "We realize it's going to take time."
